title: When does rotor cant pay on a small quadrotor co-designed with its motors and controller?
lede: research programme: fixed rotor cant on a co-designed quadrotor; cant cuts attitude error by 4.2–5.3° under INDI, geometric and PID control (10 of 10 seeds) and still wins every seed in RotorPy with canted rotors; in position hold it cuts yaw error 5–8°; on a rigid frame its side force hurts one horizontal axis (1.9–3.4× the other) whichever side the centre of pressure is on; a feed-forward from the commanded torque evens the axes but adds a rare divergence; one from the attitude integrator alone, retrained, evens them with no divergence when the integrator carries the gust torque, and runs away if bolted onto an untuned design; a linear stability test of the full loop catches every divergence (none among 4,478 flights it calls stable, ten seeds) and shows the optimiser tuned the integrator gain onto the stability boundary, so keep ki at about 0.8× its ceiling; the flights it calls unstable that hold on are contained by the 20° tilt-command limit, not the integrator clip, and diverge once that limit is raised; a describing function of that limit predicts the contained oscillation's frequency (1.44 Hz, to the FFT's resolution) and tilt amplitude (26.5° against 24.7° measured) and puts the crash limit of designs 1.25× past the ceiling at about 45°, where the simulator has it; trained with that margin as a constraint, the designs lose 0.7% in cost and stop diverging when the tilt limit is raised to 45° (0 of 384 flights against 13); a sweep of that margin finds 0.8× is the knee: 0.9× still leaves 3 of 384 flights diverging at a 45° limit, and 0.7× or 0.6× buys nothing more for the same 0.7% cost; the flights that still crash at twice the trained centre-of-pressure lever tip over because the motors run out of differential thrust: an ideal mixer with 1.25× torque removes all of them, while airmode, softer position gains or a wider crash bound do not, so the fix is thrust-to-weight above 2, not tuning; but on these airframes the endurance sizing closes only to 2.1–2.5 (mass +78%, hover power 2.4×), and a tuner given thrust-to-weight as a free variable picks 2.05–2.55 and spends it on efficiency, leaving the doubled-lever crashes in place; training across centre-of-pressure levers 0–2 halves the crashes where the designs were fragile (45 → 14–20 of 384 at lever 2, 159 → 86–87 at lever 3) by choosing heavier vehicles: mass, not thrust-to-weight, tracks robustness (ρ = −0.87 to −0.94); the retrained designs' crashes with no gust torque at a 45° tilt limit are a tilt limit they were never tuned at: all 24 are tip-overs in the first 0.8 s recovering from the 0.5 m start offset, which the 20° training limit clipped (none with the offset at 0.25 m); capping the position loop's proportional request at the lean the tune saw removes every one of those crashes without retuning (34 → 0 of 3,072 flights at 45°; 935 → 0 with the start offset doubled) for 1–2% of cost where the designs were tuned, while a tilt-rate limit makes them far worse; retraining at 45° buys nothing over that retrofit, but with the cap and a wider gain box the tuner triples the position gain and builds a 19% lighter, 30% lower-power quadrotor at the same tracking that crashes on 70% of flights if the cap is removed and 2–6× more often at twice the centre-of-pressure lever; asked to survive an uncertain centre of pressure as well, the tuner still takes a gain of about 24 s⁻² but keeps part of the mass and lengthens the frame arm, tracking best of any set and halving the lever-2 crashes of the lever-1 wide designs in one geometry, still cap-critical; a control run with the arm pinned shows the arm is not why: the robust tuner matches that robustness through mass and gains (39-46 against 52-53 crashes of 384), though on a fixed design a 4-7 mm longer arm still cuts the doubled-lever crashes by about a fifth for 4% more mass; an arm sweep on 48 fixed tunes (85-135 mm) finds crashes fall monotonically with the arm until the design stops being valid (margin test below the tuned length, mass-battery spiral above), and that a longer arm alone brings the lever-1 tune to the lever-aware designs' robustness at the same mass and power; but frame weights from 36 listed commercial frames put the cost of stretching an arm at 0.51 kg per metre (not the assumed 0.8), under which the arm buys less robustness (66 against 44 crashes at 135 mm) and runs to 150 mm before the design stops being valid, part of the arm's effect was mass, and the sizing closure turns a 20-43 g lighter frame into a 0.2-0.6 kg lighter vehicle that crashes up to twice as often; and the sizing closure itself does not hold: solved exactly rather than stopped after 60 iterations, 28 of 48 tuned designs (all six near-crash-free heavy ones) have no 15-minute fixed point, and with battery, motor and propulsive-efficiency constants taken from 405 battery listings and 29 SunnySky bench tables no design closes on LiPo, while on Li-ion they size at about 0.75 kg and their old tunes crash 3-4 times as often; swept over a 4× range of motor-lag laws (never sourced), the lever-aware and mass orderings hold but the counts and stability margins do not: with one 15 ms lag for every propeller, 19 of 24 retuned designs fail the margin test; taken from two published identifications of 5-inch quadrotors, the lag is 33-39 ms, 2.4× the assumed 15 ms: none of the 15 ms tunes passes the margin test there (359-384 of 384 flights crash), while designs retuned at 36 ms are all certified, keep the lever-aware and mass findings, and crash less than the 15 ms tunes even at 15 ms; tuned at the slow end of that range (39.1 ms) instead of its midpoint, the designs stay certified across it and crash less in every cell (not significant at six seeds); randomising the lag across that range in training instead is worse in 11 of 12 identified cells, including all four at 33 ms, so the gain is the slow training floor, not the width; tuning slower still, at 45 ms, beats the 39.1 ms tune in 19 of 20 cells including all four at 33 ms, with 22 of 24 designs still certified across the range (the two failures on the boundary), so the knee lies beyond 45 ms; at 52 and 60 ms floors, with the certificate also required at 33 ms, crashes over the identified range keep falling (236, 162, 87 of 2304 for 45, 52, 60 ms; 60 against 45 ms p = 0.004-0.014 per cell), every design stays certified, and the price is 4-8% more mass and a 20% softer position loop: no knee by 60 ms; flown through a 1 m step and a 6 m/s wind step at the design lever, the slower tunes rise 10-20% slower and overshoot a half to a third as much, settle in about the same time and drift a few millimetres more: each slower floor trades about 0.1 s of rise time for 30-50 fewer stress crashes of 1152; a 75 ms floor still crashes less inside the identified lags (29, 33 against 36, 51 of 1152, mostly not separated at six seeds) and clearly less at slower motors (49, 45 against 105, 83 at 60 ms), on a lighter vehicle, but rises 5-14% slower and settles worse: tune at 60 ms unless the motors may be slower than identified; separating the tuning floor from the ceiling shows the gain is coverage: tuned at the measured 39.1 ms lag but trained up to 150 ms, the design crashes on 27, 38 of 1152 stress flights (narrow 39.1-78.2 ms tune: 170, 178), matching the 75 ms tune; a ceiling sweep finds 100 ms not enough (82, 109 crashes against 27, 38 at 150 ms) and 200 ms free inside the measured range but far better at slow motors (50, 71 of 384 at 75 ms against 138, 131), paid in rise time (1.5 s at 100 ms, 2.0-2.3 s at 200 ms): train over at least about 4× the measured lag; a 125 ms ceiling (3.2×) gets most of the way inside the measured range (39, 62 crashes, not separated from 150 ms in 5 of 6 cells) at a 1.6 s rise, but crashes 50% more at a 75 ms motor (204, 206 against 138, 131): slow-motor robustness is close to linear in the ceiling; at ten seeds per geometry 125 ms is separated from 150 ms after all (196 against 112 identified-lag crashes of 3,840, p = 0.004), so train to about 4× the measured lag; 200 ms is not separated from 150 ms there at ten seeds (86 against 112, p = 0.08) but halves the crashes at a 75 ms motor (217 against 462 of 1,280) for 4-7% more mass; the one design in four that never settles within 5 cm of a 1 m step is the position integrator's slow pole near −ki/kp, which a three-state outer-loop model calls correctly for 96 of 96 untested designs (r 0.9995, independent of motor lag), and running the integrator only within 0.25 m of the set point removes every unsettled design (18 → 0 of 72) and halves overshoot at no cost in stress crashes (819 against 820), for a 10% slower rise; retrained with that band on, the tuner does not buy the rise back (1.83 against 1.84 s, p = 0.95): it drops integral action (ki/kp 0.057 → 0.005) and lands on the same rise-overshoot frontier, so the slower rise is the price of not overshooting; but with a 1 m set-point step added to the training objective the tuner wins all of it back (1.41 against 1.83 s, no extra crashes) by lowering the derivative gain, since under the capped proportional term rise time follows A_P/kd (Spearman 0.999), at 3-4 cm more overshoot; and a fitted-nothing point mass of the capped outer loop predicts that rise time out of sample (other caps and step sizes) within 0.04 s for steps of 1 m or more and caps up to 5 m/s², motor lag irrelevant, missing only short steps and hard caps, where one acceleration lag closes the gap; at a 45° tilt-command limit the safe start offset is an acceleration (critical offset ∝ 1/kp), and bisected over 16 start directions it is at least 4.0 m/s² / kp in every direction, longer along the axis the cant's side force helps
summary: An open research programme (target IEEE RA-L) on when a fixed rotor cant angle pays on a small quadrotor once arm, propeller, motor headroom and attitude controller are designed with it. Milestone 1 found that the torque limits of seven earlier simulated steps understated yaw authority by 2× to 2.8×; cant still beat no cant by 4.8° RMS. Milestone 2 makes roll, pitch and yaw share one thrust polytope through an attitude-priority mixer (as PX4 and Betaflight do) and puts a price on hover power. At ten seeds (extended from five, with exact Wilcoxon tests) the mixer costs 2.4° without cant and 2.3° with it, and cant's paired advantage under it is 4.98° (95% interval 3.64–5.91°, 9 of 10 seeds, p = 0.004), no larger than under a per-axis torque box (4.86°): the five-seed figure of 6.08° is withdrawn, because three of the new uncanted seeds found a second, unsaturated optimum at about 1700 W. Pricing power at 0.3° per 100 W cuts hover power 3–7× for under 0.5° of error, but the chosen cant stays at 28–37° in 19 of 20 seed-arms (best of three CMA-ES starts), refuting the hypothesis of a small 5–20° optimum; cant still wins the priced objective in 10 of 10 seeds at 0.3 and 9 of 10 at 1° per 100 W (p = 0.004). Single-start CMA-ES is unreliable on the polytope (8 of 30 seed-price cells fell to low cant, one even with power free). Milestone 4 asks whether cant only patches a weak controller: with incremental nonlinear dynamic inversion (INDI) or geometric SO(3) attitude control co-designed in place of PID (10 seeds, three CMA-ES starts each), cant still wins by 4.18° (INDI), 4.88° (geometric) and 5.27° (PID) in 10 of 10 seeds, and INDI without cant is 4.02° worse than PID with cant in 10 of 10. INDI narrows the gap by 1.1° and mostly steadies the uncanted vehicle; the chosen cant stays at a 34–35° median under every law. Simulated; TWR fixed at 2; the power price is a swept modelling choice; mass, cost and motor fits and plant ranges are inherited assumptions; no hardware. Milestone 6 adds position hold with the side force derived from the allocation (sinα / (L cosα − κ sinα) per unit roll torque, √2 smaller than an earlier study used), 6 s episodes and a 3 m/s wind step. Cant cuts yaw error by 4.7° in 6 of 6 seeds and does not buy position. Whether the side force costs position depends on the sign of the gust's disturbance torque, that is, on where the centre of pressure sits. Under the inherited sign the force opposes the drag and costs nothing (0.96×); flipped, it costs 1.21×, past the hypothesis's 20% line (re-scored, not retrained). Cant still wins the composite in 4 of 6 and 6 of 6 seeds. Milestone 6b derives the rigid-frame case: drag at a centre of pressure above or below the centre of mass gives opposite roll and pitch torque signs, which the inherited model did not have. Retrained under either geometry (6 seeds), the side force opposes the drag on one horizontal axis and adds to it on the other: late-window position error on the hurt axis is 1.9–3.4× the other axis. The typical design loses only 3% overall (median), but one seed in six diverges on 1–2 of 64 episodes. Cant still cuts yaw error by 5.1–7.7° (6 of 6) and wins the composite in 5 and 6 of 6 seeds. The translation model and the centre-of-pressure lever are inherited and assumed (lever swept 0–2×). Milestone 5 re-scores the 60 milestone-4 designs, not retuned, in RotorPy with a canted-rotor wrench, motor-speed dynamics and rotor aerodynamics scaled from its Hummingbird model. Cant still wins in 10 of 10 seeds for every law under RotorPy aerodynamics (3.1–5.8°), and the six law × cant arms keep their order (ρ 0.94–1.00; ρ 0.88–0.91 over all 60 designs against 0.95–0.97 for the stylised simulator against itself). The pre-registered top-ten test fails (ρ 0.20–0.30), but the top ten are tied and the stylised simulator scores only 0.26 against itself on fresh episodes. The stylised model is 1–2° optimistic, most for INDI. Milestone 7 lets the position loop predict the side force from its own commanded torque and lean against it (no new sensor): retrained with it, the one-axis penalty disappears (hurt/helped 1.08–1.10 against 1.91–3.41), but the term closes a loop through the motor lag that diverges on a few held-out episodes when its filter is fast (16% of episodes at 0.2 s on unretrained designs, 1.3% at 1 s), so the composite is unchanged above and worse below (J −0.33). Cant still beats no cant by 5–7° of yaw in 6 of 6 seeds. Milestone 7b feeds forward only the attitude integrator’s torque, so the proportional and derivative path no longer closes a fast loop. Retrained with it on a frame whose centre of pressure is above the centre of mass, no held-out episode diverges at the design wind (hurt/helped 0.83; 2.06 with it switched off) and fewer do out of distribution (15 against 23 of 384); below, the designs barely use their integrator (ki/kp 0.05–0.28 s−1 against 3.7–12.6) and the term is nearly inert (ratio 2.04 against 3.01) but harmless. Added to milestone 6b’s integrator-heavy designs without retraining it diverges on 23% of episodes even with no gust torque: it must come with a retune. Cant still cuts yaw error 5–8° in 6 of 6 seeds. Milestone 7c linearises the full attitude-plus-position loop (11 states, motor lag, one-step-old measurements, either feed-forward; matched to the simulator to 10−3) and tests it on 84 design-conditions × 64 held-out flights. It is a necessary test: no flight it calls stable at its own plant diverged (0 of 2,688 with the integrator feed-forward or none; 1 of 758 with the commanded-torque one), but 300 flights it calls unstable held on (accuracy 0.90 against 0.95 predicted). At ten seeds (milestone 12g) the counts are 0 of 4,478 stable flights diverging and 502 unstable ones holding on, every one of them a bolted-on design, with the same accuracy (0.902). The retrained designs’ ki/kp (3.7–4.4 s−1) sits at 0.88–1.11× the linear ceiling; the bolted-on ones at 2.3–3.4×. New designs at 0.8× their ceiling never diverge; at 1.25× the slow instability (0.5–0.7 s−1) stays bounded. Linearised about hover; the clips where divergence happens are outside the model. Milestone 7d asks what contains those unstable flights: not the attitude integrator’s clip (never reached; removing it changes no count) and not the 6 s flight length (the linear model kills 60% of them within 6 s from their initial offset alone; none diverges in 18 s flights). The 20° tilt-command limit does: raised to 45–59° (post hoc), 83–88% of the 1.25× designs’ 18 s flights diverge, close to the 96% the model calls unstable, and designs tuned onto the ceiling lose 3–4%; at 0.8× none diverges at any limit. Milestone 7aj replaces that clip by its describing function inside the same linear model: every one of the 595 unstable flight-axes of the 1.25× designs has a stable limit cycle, predicted at 1.44 Hz against 1.44 Hz measured and 26.5° of tilt against 24.7°, and the amplitude grows 1.56× from a 20° to a 30° limit against the 1.50× theory gives. The limit at which the cycle reaches 60° is a median 45.5° (285 of 640 predicted dead at 45° against 535 simulated). It undercounts near the knee because it leaves out the start offset, wind step and noise. Post hoc, above 20° the certificate stops being necessary: at 45°, 29 of the 31 deaths of on-ceiling tunes are at plants it calls stable. Milestone 7e trains with the margin as a CMA-ES constraint (ki ≤ 0.8× ceiling at every plant corner): the centre-of-pressure-above designs land on it and lose 0.011 in held-out cost (about 0.7%); at a 45–59° tilt limit they diverge on 0 of 384 flights against 13 for the unconstrained designs, and at twice the trained lever on 4 against 15. With the centre of pressure below the constraint barely binds and changes nothing. Milestone 7f sweeps that bound (1.0×, 0.9×, 0.8×, 0.7×, 0.6× of the ceiling; 48 new CMA-ES runs): at a 45° tilt limit the designs diverge on 9, 3, 0, 0 and 0 of 384 held-out flights (unconstrained 13), and at twice the trained lever the counts reach a floor at 0.8×; the cost penalty is about 0.011 at every bound from 0.9× down, so 0.8× is the knee and tighter margins buy nothing. At ten seeds (milestone 12b, exact Wilcoxon tests) the counts are 19, 6, 1, 1 and 0 of 640 (unconstrained 31), every arm from 0.8× down beats the unconstrained tune in 10 of 10 seeds (p = 0.002), and two of ten unconstrained tunes diverge even at the 20° limit they were trained at, where no constrained design does; the penalty, over the 8 seeds whose unconstrained tune stayed stable, is 0.012 (0.8%, p = 0.008). Milestone 7g asks why designs inside that margin still crash at twice the trained lever (12 and 37 of 1,152 flights at 20° and 45° limits; 45 and 55 of 384 with the centre of pressure below). Every one tips past 60° while the attitude-priority mixer is saturated and the gust torque nears the motors' limit. An idealised mixer removes two thirds; with 1.25× torque room (1.5× below), all. A wider crash bound, halved position gains or an airmode mixer do not, so the residual is a thrust-headroom limit (thrust-to-weight 2 is assumed), not a stability one. At ten seeds per set (milestone 12f) the diagnosis holds: an ideal mixer cuts the three margin-trained sets from 69 to 13 of 1,920 at 45° (29 of 30 designs better, Wilcoxon p < 10−5), 1.25× torque takes them to 0 but leaves 8–9 of 640 below, 1.5× takes every set to 0, and airmode is slightly worse (69 to 75, p = 0.03). Milestone 7h makes thrust-to-weight a design variable. On the co-designed airframes the 15-minute endurance sizing closes only up to 2.1–2.5: re-sized there, 7e’s designs lose every doubled-lever crash (4 and 12 → 0 above; 45 and 55 → 0 and 2 below) but weigh 78% more and hover on 2.4× the power. Retrained with thrust-to-weight free (1.5–4), all 12 seeds pick 2.05–2.55 and spend the headroom on larger propellers and lower hover power, not torque, so the doubled-lever crashes stay (9 against 4 above, 38 against 45 below). Milestone 7i trains across centre-of-pressure levers 0–2. Where the old designs were fragile (below), doubled-lever crashes fall from 45 to 14–20 of 384 and tripled-lever crashes from 159 to 86–87, at no cost at the design lever; where they were robust (above), nothing changes. Free thrust-to-weight adds nothing: what the tuner buys is mass, which at fixed thrust-to-weight brings bigger motors while the gust torque stays put (post hoc, mass ranks with tripled-lever crashes at ρ = −0.87 above and −0.94 below; thrust-to-weight at +0.08 and −0.02). Milestone 7j explains the crashes the retrained designs show with no gust torque at PX4’s 45° tilt limit (24 of 1,152 flights, 0 for 7e): every one is a tip-over in the first 0.8 s, recovering from the 0.5 m start offset with a position gain at its search bound; the 20° limit used in training clipped that lean. Halving the offset, an ideal mixer or halved position gains remove all of them. Tune at the tilt limit you fly. Milestone 7k fixes it in the controller instead: capping the position error in the proportional term at 0.25–0.35 m (the 20° lean the tune saw) or ramping the setpoint removes every transient crash at 45° (34 → 0 of 3,072 flights; 935 → 0 with a 1.0 m offset) for 1–2% of held-out cost at 20°; a tilt-rate limit of 0.5–1 rad/s makes it far worse (up to 515), and PX4’s tilt-magnitude cone changes nothing at the trained offset. Milestone 7l retrains at 45°: alone it lands on the 20° tune’s cost and its crashes at a 1.0 m offset (92–103 of 384, which the cap removes); with the cap and the position-gain box widened from 10 to 31.6 s−2, the tuner picks gains of 22–31 s−2 and a 11–19% lighter airframe with 18–30% less hover power at the same held-out tracking, but those designs crash on 267–274 of 384 flights without the cap and on 73–105 (against 12–52) at twice the centre-of-pressure lever. Milestone 7m adds the lever-aware objective to that wide box: the tuner still picks 20–31 s−2, but its designs weigh 1.40–1.45 kg (between the lever-1 wide designs’ 1.10–1.29 and the old box’s 1.53–1.60) and have the longest frame arms and highest torque per weight of any set, track best at the trained levers, and crash on 52–53 of 384 flights at twice the lever (against 73–105), but 231–250 without the cap. Milestone 7n pins the arm at the lever-1 designs’ length and retrains: the lever-aware designs crash on 39–46 of 384 at twice the lever, no more than with the arm free, reaching it through mass and gains; on a fixed design, a 4–7 mm longer arm cuts those crashes by about a fifth (73→59, 105→87) for 4% more mass, since frame mass grows with the arm. Milestone 7o sweeps the arm from 85 to 135 mm on 48 fixed designs: crashes at twice the lever fall monotonically with the arm wherever the design stays valid (lever-1 designs 73→6 and 105→44 of 384), with no interior optimum; the limits are the stability margin below the tuned length and the mass–battery spiral above it (+26% to +98% mass by 120–135 mm); the growing gust exposure takes back up to a third of the gain; and on the lever-1 tune a longer arm alone matches the lever-aware designs’ robustness at the same mass, power and tracking. The motor-mass and sizing fits are inherited assumptions. Milestone 7p sources the frame-mass law from 36 listed commercial frames (one retailer, verbatim spec lines): stretching one frame design adds 0.51 kg per metre of arm (0.26 g per mm of wheelbase), 64% of the assumed 0.8, while across brands a frame designed for a larger size weighs 2.27 kg/m more. Re-swept under these laws without retraining, crashes still fall monotonically with the arm, but with the stretched-design slope much more slowly (lever-1 designs, centre of pressure below: 66 against 44 of 384 at 135 mm), and the arm stays valid to 150 mm instead of 130 (above). At a fixed arm the heavier law crashes less on 253 of 350 design-points, so part of 7o’s arm effect was mass. The inherited endurance closure multiplies frame mass 6–15×: the cross-brand law’s 20–43 g lighter frames make the sized vehicles 0.18–0.64 kg lighter, and on the same tunes they crash on 151–160 of 384 flights instead of 73–105. Milestone 7q checks the endurance sizing closure itself. Solved exactly instead of by a damped iteration stopped after 60 steps, 28 of the 48 tuned designs, including all six heavy (≥ 1.7 kg), near-crash-free ones, have no fixed point at 15 minutes: the tuners sat every design on the closure’s edge. Listed components move all three inherited constants: LiPo packs store 132 Wh/kg (assumed 150; 140 packs), 5-inch propulsion converts 0.426 of electrical power into ideal momentum power (assumed 0.4875; SunnySky bench tables), and motors weigh 0.58 of the assumed law (33 motors). With all three, no design closes on LiPo (longest closing endurance 11.9–13.0 min); on Li-ion (210 Wh/kg) all close at about 0.75 kg, and on their old tunes they crash on 20–33 more of 64 flights per design at twice the centre-of-pressure lever. Listings, not measurements. Retuned on the sourced Li-ion closure (milestone 7r, 48 CMA-ES runs), the tuners do not keep the 0.75 kg vehicle: they shrink the propeller (0.13 → 0.11 m), draw more hover power and size back to 0.99–1.29 kg on the closure’s edge, and robustness again follows mass on one curve: the lever-aware objective crashes on 54 and 64 of 384 flights at twice the lever and a 45° tilt limit against 106 and 131 for the lever-1 objective, and is 14–24% heavier. The mass-robustness relation is not an artefact of the truncated solve; the inherited power price and fixed 15-minute endurance now set the mass. Swept over nine motor-lag laws (7.5–30 ms at 5 inches, diameter exponent 0–3; milestone 7s, not retuned), the orderings survive (lever-aware beats lever-1 under all nine; ρ(mass, crashes) −0.68 to −0.93 up to 15 ms), but the counts do not: with one 15 ms lag for every propeller the retuned lever-aware designs crash on 85 and 92 of 384 flights against 51 and 53 for the published ones, only 5 of 24 retuned designs pass the stability-margin test, and at 30 ms one design of 72 does. The lag law is assumed, not sourced. Taken from two published system identifications of 5–5.1 inch quadrotors (33 and 39.1 ms; milestone 7t), the lag is 2.4× the assumed value: at it none of the 24 designs tuned at 15 ms passes the margin test and they crash on 359–384 of 384 flights, while designs retuned at 36 ms all pass, crash on 63–161, keep the lever-aware advantage (+14–28% mass), and crash less than the 15 ms tunes even at 15 ms (8–59 against 54–131). The two identifications come from one lab and the diameter exponent is not sourced. Milestone 7u retunes at the slower identification (39.1 ms) instead of the midpoint: inside the identified range those designs crash less than the 36 ms ones under all three lags in all four arm-geometries, even at 36 ms (109, 132, 61, 59 against 149, 161, 63, 82 of 384), all 24 stay certified at 33–39.1 ms (20 of 24 midpoint designs do), at the same mass. Every cell leans the same way but none is significant at six seeds (Mann–Whitney p 0.08–0.81); the price is a lost certificate on 4 of 6 designs of one set at the old 15 ms law. With only a range for the motor lag, tune at its slow end. Milestone 7v randomised the training lag across 33–39.1 ms instead (certified at both ends): those designs crash more than the slow-end ones in 11 of 12 law × arm-geometry cells, including all four at 33 ms (101, 112, 61, 53 against 80, 107, 37, 46 of 384), and land between the midpoint and slow-end tunes; not significant per cell at six seeds (sign test p = 0.125). Train on plants no faster than the slow end. Milestone 7w tuned slower still, at 45 ms (unsourced, beyond the slower identification): those designs crash less than the 39.1 ms tunes in 19 of 20 law × arm-geometry cells (one tie), including all four at 33 ms (75, 77, 27, 34 against 80, 107, 37, 46 of 384), 21–29% fewer over the identified range, at the same mass; 22 of 24 stay certified across 33–39.1 ms (the two failures sit on the boundary, ρ ≤ 1.0002). Sign test p = 0.125 at every lag. No knee yet: tune slower than the slowest measurement, limited by the certificate at the fast end. Milestone 7x tuned the lever-aware objective at 52 and 60 ms (unsourced floors), with the certificate also required at 33 ms: crashes over the identified range keep falling (348, 236, 162, 87 of 2304 for 39.1, 45, 52 and 60 ms tunes; 8 and 12 against 27 and 34 of 384 at 33 ms for 60 against 45 ms), the 60 against 45 ms gap is measured (Mann–Whitney p = 0.004–0.014 in all six identified cells), and all 24 designs stay certified, the 33 ms corner slack on 22 of them. No knee by 60 ms; the price is 4–8% more mass, a 20% softer position loop and about 5% worse tracking, so the floor is a mass and tracking choice, not a stability one. Simulated; the stress test (twice the trained lever, 45°) favours a slow, heavy vehicle. Milestone 7y prices that softer loop without retraining: flown through a 1 m position step and a calm-to-wind step at the design lever, the 39.1, 45, 52 and 60 ms tunes rise to 90% in 1.44, 1.58, 1.64, 1.74 s (centre of pressure above; 1.39–1.77 s below) and overshoot 6.4, 5.9, 3.8, 3.2 cm (9.7–2.7 below), monotone in every cell; settle time to 5 cm barely moves (+16% above, −24% below for 60 against 45 ms), and peak drift after a 6 m/s wind step grows by 4–5 mm. In calm air the motor lag itself changes nothing; 8 of 48 designs carry a slow final approach (position gain 4.5–9.7 s−2) whatever the floor. Milestone 7z adds a 75 ms floor: inside the identified lags it crashes on 29, 33 of 1152 stress flights against the 60 ms tune's 36, 51 (not separated at six seeds in five of six cells), and clearly fewer at slower flown lags (49, 45 against 105, 83 at 60 ms; p = 0.010–0.026 in three of four cells at 60 and 75 ms); the designs are lighter (1.43 against 1.47–1.51 kg) and all certified, but rise 5–14% slower, overshoot more (4.8, 3.2 against 3.2, 2.7 cm) and settle later, so 60 ms stays the tune for motors near the identifications. Milestone 7aa separates the tuning floor from the ceiling: trained at the measured 39.1 ms floor with lags up to 150 ms, the designs crash on 27, 38 of 1152 identified-lag stress flights against 170, 178 for the 39.1–78.2 ms tune (p = 0.002–0.005 in all 12 cells) and are not separated from the 75 ms tune anywhere, with no faster rise (2.23, 1.76 s): the robustness of the slower tunes came from covering slow plants, not from leaving out fast ones. Milestone 7ab sweeps that ceiling at the same floor: 100 ms leaves 82, 109 identified-lag crashes (more than 150 ms in 11 of 12 cells, p = 0.002–0.046), while 200 ms is not separated from 150 ms inside the measured lags (17, 36) and crashes far less at a 75 ms motor (50, 71 of 384 against 138, 131); the price is rise time (1.47, 1.54 s at 100 ms; 2.02, 2.27 s at 200 ms), 5–7% more mass and a slower final approach, so the ceiling is a dial between robustness to unmeasured slow motors and response, with the knee between 100 and 150 ms (about 4× the measured lag). Milestone 7ac places that knee with a 125 ms ceiling: identified-lag crashes 39, 62 (between 100 ms’s 82, 109 and 150 ms’s 27, 38, separated from 150 ms in 1 of 6 cells), rise 1.57, 1.65 s (faster than 150 ms above, p = 0.026), but at a 75 ms motor 204, 206 of 384 crashes against 138, 131 (p = 0.010, 0.011): the curve is a slope, not a cliff, slow-motor robustness falls almost linearly with the ceiling, and 5 of 12 125 ms designs never settle within 5 cm. Simulated; the ceilings are brackets, not sourced. Milestone 7ad traced the designs that never settle on a 1 m step (18 of 72) to the position integrator’s slow pole near −ki/kp: a three-state outer-loop model calls all 96 untested designs correctly (r 0.9995), and integrating only within 0.25 m of the set point removes every unsettled design and halves overshoot with stress crashes unchanged (819 against 820), for a 10% slower rise (simulated). Milestone 7ae retrained the 125 ms tune with that band on: the tuner kept kp and kd, cut ki/kp about tenfold (0.057 → 0.005 s−1) and did not recover the rise time (1.83 against 1.84 s, p = 0.95); every design settles and stays certified, with crashes not separated (simulated, six seeds per geometry). Milestone 7af added a 1 m set-point step to the training objective (band on): the tuner won the rise time back and more (1.41 against 1.83 s, p = 3.7×10−5) by lowering kd (6.5 → 4.7 s−1), with crashes unchanged (97 against 107 of 2,304) and every design certified and settled, at 4.7–5.3 cm overshoot against 1.1–1.8. Under the capped proportional term the vehicle cruises at about AP/kd, and rise time follows kd with Spearman ρ = 0.999 over 36 designs (simulated, six seeds per geometry, one unsourced step weight). Milestone 7ag flew those 36 designs again at caps of 2–8 m/s2 and steps of 0.5–2 m (756 flights): a one-dimensional point mass of the capped, gated outer loop with no fitted constant predicts each design’s rise within 0.10 s for 35–36 of 36 at caps up to 5 m/s2 and steps of 1–2 m (median error 0.002–0.040 s), better than 7af’s fitted line in every out-of-sample condition; the 33–39.1 ms motor laws move no rise by more than 0.05 s. It misses at a 0.5 m step (31 of 36) and an 8 m/s2 cap (23 of 36), where the late braking lean makes the drone faster; one 135 ms acceleration lag fitted on the in-sample condition (post hoc) brings those to 36 and 33 of 36 (simulated, one evaluation seed). Milestones 12c–12e reran the knee of that sweep at ten seeds per geometry (predictions committed before each run): identified-lag crashes fall 326 / 196 / 112 / 86 of 3,840 at 100 / 125 / 150 / 200 ms, with 100→125 ms (p = 0.04, paired p = 0.001) and 125→150 ms (p = 0.004) separated and 150→200 ms not (p = 0.08), so the training ceiling should sit at about 4× the slowest identified lag; 100 ms saves only 3–4% mass and 0.1–0.15 s of rise against 125 ms (simulated). Milestones 7am–7an: at a 45° tilt-command limit the start offset a design survives scales as 1/kp (AUC 0.985 for kp · |e| against 0.910 for |e|); bisected to 3 mm along 16 directions for 36 designs × 64 plants, the guaranteed radius is at least 4.0 m/s² / kp, the cant's side force makes it 1.77× its mean along one axis (symmetric with the force switched off), and a 3.5 m/s² acceleration cap keeps all but 9 of 55,296 flights alive from 3 m (simulated).
